messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 74-year-old retired welder, married for over fifty years, who came to the clinic at his wife’s urging after years of silent suffering. He was born in a small village in Vietnam and lived through the war as a civilian. One afternoon in 1968, during what he later learned was a bombing run by American planes, he was caught outside his home. The explosions threw him into a ditch, and he lay there for hours, choking on dust and smoke, unable to draw a full breath while the ground shuddered with each impact. He remembers fragments—the smell of burning thatch, the screaming of a neighbor’s water buffalo—but much of that day remains a jumble of disconnected sensations. The memory feels alien to him, as if it happened to someone else, and the story itself seems too extreme to be real; he has sometimes wondered if he imagined it all.

After the war, Minh moved to the United States, became a welder, and raised a family. But the old sensations never fully left him. Certain car sounds—the rumble of a heavy engine or a backfire—would jerk him back to that ditch. When that happened, his memory would surge, not as a complete narrative but as visceral fragments: the pressure of the dirt, the terror of not being able to breathe. He learned to redirect his thoughts quickly, forcing himself to think of something neutral—his workbench, the blue sky—to shut the intrusion down. He also began to avoid talking about the war altogether. What was the point? The people responsible had never faced any consequences, and he had come to believe that the event happened partly because he had not run fast enough or hidden better. That sense of injustice and self-blame made the memory even harder to discuss, so he stayed silent.

Over the decades, Minh found himself avoiding open spaces, especially fields or parking lots that felt exposed; he would walk along walls or stay close to buildings. The breathlessness—any feeling of being short of air, even from climbing stairs—would immediately trigger a flash of that afternoon, and he would become hypervigilant, scanning his surroundings for threats. He had difficulty concentrating at work because his mind was constantly on alert, and at night he struggled to fall asleep, needing to stay vigilant even in his own bedroom. The hypervigilance itself made him more sensitive to car sounds—every distant engine became a potential danger signal, which in turn triggered more intrusive memories.

Minh’s wife noticed that he would sometimes stare at the television during war documentaries, then turn away without a word. Media coverage of conflicts anywhere in the world would resurrect that hollow feeling of his memory being incomplete, and he would retreat into redirection again. But avoiding these triggers only reinforced his sense that the event was too terrible to integrate, and the memory remained fragmented and alien. The self-blame deepened: if he had acted differently, perhaps he would have a complete memory, something that made sense. He had long felt that nothing had been done about the injustice, and that belief kept him on guard, ready for the next car sound, the next struggle for breath.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a panic attack in a supermarket parking lot when a truck backfired. He dropped to his knees, gasping, unable to speak, and his wife had to drive him home. That night, lying awake and alert, he realized he could no longer manage this on his own. He is afraid of what talking might do—that it will make the memory more real, or that he will be overcome by shame. But he also hopes, quietly, that perhaps there is a way to make the memory feel like his own, and to finally catch a full breath.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that the trauma memory directly causes triggers; instead, hypervigilance (threat) increases sensitivity to triggers, but the memory itself does not drive the occurrence or salience of triggers.
